title.en: Hwanung Descends to Mount Taebak

region.zh: 妙香山，平安北道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2332 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the primeval ages the divine being Hwanin (Che-so, the Creator) permits his son Hwanung, weary of heaven, to descend and found a mundane kingdom. With three thousand spirit companions he alights on Mount Taebak, gathers his followers under an ancient pak-tal tree, proclaims himself King of the Universe, and governs through three viceregents: the Wind General, the Rain Governor, and the Cloud Teacher.
summary.zh: 太初之世，神人桓因（帝釋）允許其子桓雄厭倦天界、下凡建國。桓雄率三千從神降於太白山，聚眾神於古檀樹下，自稱天王，以風伯、雨師、雲師三輔臣治理天下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition retold by a 1905 Western historian; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the primeval ages, so the story runs, there was a divine being named Whan-in, or Che-so, the Creator. His son, Whan-ung, being affected by a celestial weariness, obtained permission to descend to the earth and found a mundane kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Armed with this warrant, Whan-ung with three thousand spirit companions descended upon Ta-bak Mountain, the mountain now known as Myo-hyang San in Pyongan Province. It was in the twenty-fifth year of the Emperor Yao of China, a date the annals set at 2332 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He gathered his spirit friends beneath the shade of an ancient sandalwood tree, and there proclaimed himself King of the Universe. He governed through his three vice-regents, the Wind General, the Rain Governor, and the Cloud Teacher; but as he had not yet taken human shape, he found it difficult to assume control of a purely human kingdom, and so searched for a means of incarnation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ungnyeo and the Breath of the Wind

region.zh: 檀木山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 2332 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Having endured the cave ordeal and become a perfect woman, the bear Ungnyeo's first wish is motherhood, and she cries out for a son. Hwanung, the Spirit King, passing on the wind beholds her sitting beside the stream; he circles round her, breathes upon her, and her cry is answered. She cradles the babe in moss beneath the sandalwood tree.
summary.zh: 熊女忍過洞中苦行化為完美女子後，初願是為人母，呼求賜子。桓雄乘風而過，見其坐於溪畔，繞行其身，噓氣吹拂，其願得償。她將嬰兒安置於檀樹下的苔蘚中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; the conception-by-wind episode parallels Greek cloud-shaped unions (cf. Danae) and is tagged interpretively.

passages.text: At early dawn a tiger and a bear met upon the mountainside and held a colloquy: would that they might become men. Whan-ung overheard them, and a voice from the void bade each eat twenty garlics and a piece of artemisia and retire from the sun's light for thrice seven days. The tiger, fierce by nature, broke the restraint and came out early; the bear waited in faith and stepped forth a perfect woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first wish of the bear-woman's heart was maternity, and she cried, 'Give me a son.' Whan-ung, the Spirit King, passing on the wind, beheld her sitting beside the stream. He circled round her, breathed upon her, and her cry was answered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: She cradled her babe in moss beneath that same sandalwood tree, and it was there that in after years the wild people of the country found the child sitting, and made him their king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Teaches the Nine Wild Tribes

region.zh: 平壤古都（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 2333 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: The child found under the sandalwood tree, Dangun Wanggeom, Lord of the Pak-tal Tree, is made king over the nine wild tribes (Ku-i) who love drink, dancing and song. He teaches them the relation of king and subject, the rite of marriage, cooking, house-building, the binding of the hair, the cutting of trees and the tilling of fields, and makes Pyongyang his capital.
summary.zh: 檀樹下所生的檀君王儉（檀木之主）為九夷之首領。九夷嗜酒善歌舞，以草織為衣，穴居野處。檀君教以君臣之義、婚姻之禮、烹飪築室之術、束髮之俗、伐木墾田之法，並定都平壤。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The babe was the Tan-gun, the Lord of the Pak-tal Tree, also less widely known as Wang-gum. At that time the country was peopled by the nine wild tribes commonly called the Ku-i: the Kyun, Pang, Whang, Fak, Chuk, Hyun, P'ung, Yang and U.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: These aborigines were fond of drinking, dancing and singing. They dressed in woven grass and ate nuts, roots and berries; in summer they lived beneath the trees, in winter in a rudely covered hole in the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Tan-gun became their king he taught them the relation of king and subject, the rite of marriage, the art of cooking and the science of house-building. He taught them to bind up the hair with a cloth about the head, to cut down trees and to till fields. He made P'yung-yang the capital of his kingdom, and there tradition says he reigned until the coming of Ki-ja in 1122 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Raises the Altar on Mari-san

region.zh: 摩離山，江華島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2265 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: In 2265 BC Dangun offers the first sacrifice at Hyul-gu on the island of Kang-wha, building a stone altar on Mari-san that remains to this day. The people call it Tan-gun's Altar, or the Ch'am-sung Altar; nearby stands the Sam-nang fortress said to have been built by Dangun's three sons, and at Mun-wha a shrine honors the Korean trinity of Whan-in, Whan-ung and Tan-gun.
summary.zh: 公元前2265年，檀君首祭於江華島血谷，並在摩離山上築石壇，至今猶存。民稱之為檀君壇，又名朝天壇；鄰近峻德城相傳為檀君三子所築，牡室又有桓因、桓雄、檀君三聖祠。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; the altar remains a site of modern veneration; presented as historical record.

passages.text: We learn that in 2265 BC the Tan-gun first offered sacrifice at Hyul-gu on the island of Kang-wha. For this purpose he built an altar on Mari San which remains to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the top of Mari San is a stone platform or altar known as the Tan-gun's Altar, popularly believed to have been used by the Tan-gun four thousand years ago; it is called also the Ch'am-sung Altar. On Chun-dung San there is a fortress called Sam-nang, believed to have been built by the Tan-gun's three sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Mun-wha there is a shrine to the Korean trinity, Whan-in, Whan-ung and Tan-gun; and though the Tan-gun later resumed his spirit form, his grave is still shown at Kang-dong, four hundred and ten feet in circumference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Retires to Kuwol-san and Becomes Spirit

region.zh: 不注山，黃海道月嶽（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Upon the arrival of the sage Ki-ja at Pyongyang, Dangun withdraws to Ku-wul San, the old Korean A-sa-dal, in present Mun-wha. There he resumes his spirit form and disappears forever from the earth, ending the Dangun line and clearing the way for the Ki-ja dynasty.
summary.zh: 箕子東來之際，檀君退隱於不注山（古稱阿斯達，在今黃海道牡室），復其神形，永離人間，檀君之世遂終，箕子朝鮮開端。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: It is said that upon the arrival of Ki-ja, the Tan-gun retired to Ku-wul San, known in pure Korean as A-sa-dal, in the present town of Mun-wha in Whang-ha Province.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: There he resumed his spirit form and disappeared forever from the earth. His wife, tradition adds, was a woman of Pi-so-ap, whose location is unknown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tan-gun's kingdom is generally believed to have extended from Mun-gyung in the south to the Heuk-yong River in the north, and from the Japan Sea in the east to Yo-ha in the west; and the word Tan-gun, some think, refers to a line of native chieftains who antedated the coming of Ki-ja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Dangun Sends Puru to the Court of the Great Yu

region.zh: 塗山會盟，阿穆爾河谷（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 2187 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: When the great Ha-u-si (Yu the Great), who drained the waters covering the interior of China, summoned all vassal kings to his court at To-san, Dangun sent his son Puru as envoy. Another work affirms that when Ki-ja later came to Korea, Puru fled northward and founded the kingdom of North Pu-yu, which later moved and became Eastern Pu-yu.
summary.zh: 大禹疏九河、會諸侯於塗山時，檀君遣其子夫婁為使入貢。另一說謂箕子東來後，夫婁北走而建立北夫餘，後遷都為東夫餘。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition with conflicting dates; Hulbert himself flags the discrepancies.

passages.text: When the great Ha-u-si, who drained off the waters which covered the interior of China, called to his court at To-san all the vassal kings, the Tan-gun sent his son, Pu-ru, as an envoy. This was supposed to be in the year 2187 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another work affirms that when Ki-ja came to Korea, Pu-ru fled northward and founded the kingdom of North Pu-yu, which at a later date moved to Ka-yup-wun and became Eastern Pu-yu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: These stories show such enormous discrepancies in dates that they are alike incredible, and yet it may be that the latter story has some basis in fact; at any rate it gives us our only clue to the founding of the kingdom of Pu-yu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: P'ang-o, Warden of Roads and Waters

region.zh: 牛首州，春川（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gojoseon annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated late Dangun dynasty

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Late in the Dangun dynasty a minister named P'ang-o holds special charge of road-making and drainage. One authority says the Emperor of China ordered P'ang-o to cut a road between the eastern tribe Ye-mak and Cho-sun; a stone tablet to P'ang-o stands at Ox-hair Town, the old U-su-ju near Chun-ch'un, whose Ox-head Plain still confirms the ancient name.
summary.zh: 檀君朝末年有大臣逄蒙，專司修路治水。一說中國天子命逄蒙開濊貊與朝鮮間之通道。春川古稱牛首州，今尚有牛頭坪，並立逄蒙石碑以紀其事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Late in the Tan-gun dynasty there was a minister named P'ang-o who is said to have had as his special charge the making of roads and the care of drainage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: One authority says that the Emperor of China ordered P'ang-o to cut a road between Ye-mak, an eastern tribe, and Cho-sun. From this we see that, according to some authorities, the word Cho-sun antedates the coming of Ki-ja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The town of Chun-ch'un, fifty miles east of Seoul, was known in this period as U-su-ju, Ox-hair Town, and a plot of ground there is still called the U-du-bol, Ox-head Plain, where a stone tablet to P'ang-o is erected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Tal-geui the Nine-Tailed Fox

region.zh: 西嶺山洞（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Shang-dynasty legend carried in Korean annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1050 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: The emperor's concubine Tal-geui is so beautiful that whoever she smiles upon is enslaved. The statesman Pi-gan, suspecting a fox that has drunk from a twenty-year-old skull, has detectives track her to a mountain cave where foxes fawn upon her, and slays her kin. Robed in their white breast-fur, he unmasks her at court: when he dies by her demand, he curses her to resume her true form — a white fox with nine tails — and she leaps from the window and escapes.
summary.zh: 紂王寵姬妲己美艷無雙，笑則媚人。比干疑其為飲枯顱之水而得人形之狐，遣偵探跡其獨登之山洞，見群狐獻媚，遂盡誅之，剝其胸前白毛為裘。妲己知親族已死，以媚惑帝求剖比干之心以驗七竅；比干臨刑斥其現形，頃刻毛髮怒長，化為九尾白狐，破窗而遁。

sensitivity.note: The kumiho (nine-tailed fox) motif is one of Korea's defining folklore figures; tagged with the fox-woman transformation sense of 'transformation'.

passages.text: The concubine Tal-geui was wonderfully beautiful, but surpassingly so when she smiled. At such times the person upon whom she smiled was fascinated as by a serpent and forced to comply with whatever request she made. Pondering this, Pi-gan decided that she must be a fox in human shape, for it is well known that if an animal tastes of water that has lain twenty years in a human skull it acquires the power to assume human shape at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Inquiries showed that monthly she ascended a certain mountain alone, leaving her attendants at the foot. Armed detectives followed her unseen and saw her enter a cave near the summit; she emerged accompanied by a pack of foxes who leaped and fawned upon her. When she left, the spies entered, put the foxes to the sword, and cut from each body the piece of white fur always found on the breast of the fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Tal-geui next met the emperor, dressed in a sumptuous white fur robe, she shuddered but did not guess the truth, until a month later, entering the cave, she beheld the festering remains of her kindred. Adorning herself in all her finery she exerted her fascination to the utmost, and when the net was well woven about the royal dupe she said: 'I hear there are seven orifices in the heart of every good man. I fain would put it to the test. I would see the heart of Pi-gan.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the executioner's knife was plunged into the victim's breast, Pi-gan cried: 'You are no woman; you are a fox in disguise, and I charge you to resume your natural shape.' Instantly hair sprang forth upon her face, her nails grew long, and bursting from her garments she stood revealed, a white fox with nine tails. With one parting snarl at the assembled court she leaped from the window and made good her escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja and the Great-Law from the Tortoise

region.zh: 洛水（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Shang-Zhou legend carried in Korean annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Before emigrating east, the imprisoned sage Ki-ja presents Emperor Mu-wang with the Hong-bum, the Great-Law, found long before inscribed on the back of a fabled tortoise that rose from the waters of the Nak River in the days of Ha-u-si — a text no one had been able to decipher until Ki-ja took it in hand. Then with five thousand followers he passes eastward into the peninsula.
summary.zh: 箕子囚於獄，武王釋之而求道。箕子乃以《洪範》獻王——相傳此大法初見於大禹時洛水神龜背上之文，千載無人能解，至箕子始通其義。遂率五千眾東渡朝鮮。

sensitivity.note: Legend of the Chinese classic Hongfan as transmitted in Korean historiography; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Ki-ja, sole survivor of the great trio of statesmen, had saved his life only by feigning madness, and was now in prison; but Mu-wang came to his door and besought him to become Prime Minister. Loyalty to the fallen dynasty compelled him to refuse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He secured the Emperor's consent to his plan of emigrating to Cho-sun, but before setting out he presented the Emperor with that great work, the Hong-bum or Great-Law, which had been found inscribed upon the back of the fabled tortoise that came up out of the waters of the Nak River in the days of Ha-u-si over a thousand years before, and which no one had been able to decipher till Ki-ja took it in hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then with his five thousand followers he passed eastward into the peninsula of Korea, to found a kingdom that would last almost a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja Plants a Kingdom of Five Thousand

region.zh: 平壤（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ki-ja Choson legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1122 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Ki-ja settles at Pyongyang, the old Dangun capital, bringing the principles of history and poetry, the sciences of manners, music, medicine and incantation, and teachers of a hundred useful trades. His short penal code matches crime to punishment; a clay broad-brim hat keeps quarrelsome males at arm's length; the well-field system yields a ninth of the harvest; and willows planted along the Ta-dong give the city a name of peace.
summary.zh: 箕子都平壤，率五千移民，攜詩書之教、禮樂醫巫之學、百工之技。立法簡嚴：殺人者償、爭訟者罰穀、盜者沒為奴而可贖。又製陶冠以杜鬥毆，行井田九一之貢，沿大同江植柳萬株，民呼其水為朝鮮之黃河。

sensitivity.note: Ki-ja (Jizi) founding is a historiographic legend, contested by modern scholarship; recorded here as myth-history.

passages.text: In whatever way he came, Ki-ja finally settled at the town of P'yung-yang which had already been the capital of the Tan-gun dynasty. He found the country semi-barbarous, and the reforms he instituted give abundant evidence of his genius.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: His penal code was short: murder was punished with death inflicted in the same manner as the crime; brawling was punished by a fine paid in grain; theft was punished by enslaving the offender, who could regain freedom by a heavy fine. To prevent quarrelling, it is said, he compelled all males to wear a broad-brimmed hat of clay pasted on a framework; if the hat was doffed or broken the offender was severely punished, which kept the men at arm's length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He picked men from the various districts, trained them in the duties of government, reduced the language of the people to writing, and taught the arts and sciences he had brought. All arable land was divided into squares of nine parts; whoever cultivated the eight surrounding squares must also till the central one for the government, which received a ninth of the produce. Prosperity was seen on every side, and the people called the Ta-dong River the Yellow River of Korea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ki-ja Weeps in the Barley Field

region.en: Ruins of the Shang capital, China (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 殷墟（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Zhou-era elegy tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1120 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: Though made King of Cho-sun without vassalage, Ki-ja is permitted to send envoys to worship at the tombs of the fallen Shang. He visits the site of the ancient capital himself, finds it sown with barley, and weeps, composing an elegy on the spot before going on to swear allegiance to the new emperor — an act the Cho-so history calls his weakness, for he had sworn never to do so.
summary.zh: 武王封箕子於朝鮮而不臣。箕子嘗遣使祭殷墓，又親往殷墟，見宮室毀壞、生禾黍，悲而作《麥秀歌》，後乃朝周。史稱此為其弱點，蓋曾誓不仕周也。

sensitivity.note: Classic Chinese elegy tradition (Maixiu ge) embedded in Korean annals; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: From the very first Korea was an independent kingdom, for though Emperor Mu-wang made Ki-ja King of Cho-sun he neither demanded nor received his allegiance as vassal, and even allowed Ki-ja to send envoys to worship at the tombs of the fallen dynasty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is said that Ki-ja himself visited the site of the ancient Shang capital, but when he found it sown with barley he wept and composed an elegy on the occasion, after which he went and swore allegiance to the new Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The work entitled Cho-so says that he mounted a white cart drawn by a white horse and went to the new capital and swore allegiance; and it adds that in this he showed his weakness, for he had sworn never to do so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Luminous Egg of Hyokkose

region.zh: 新羅都城慶州（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Silla founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 57 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The chiefs of six Chin-han states meet and merge their fiefs into a kingdom with its capital Su-ya-bul, near modern Kyongju. On the mountainside revellers behold a ball of light on which a white horse stands grazing; as they approach, the horse rises into the air and vanishes, leaving a great luminous egg. It opens of itself and discloses a handsome boy, amid vivid light and thunder, who is set on the throne as Hyokkose.
summary.zh: 辰韓六部酋長會盟，併為一國，都於徐耶伐（今慶州）。會中有眾見山上白光如月，中有白馬伏跪；眾近之，馬凌空而沒，餘一大卵。俄而卵自開，出一俊秀男嬰，光芒燦然，雷聲震地。眾立為王，是為朴赫居世。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic founding legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the year 57 BC the chiefs of the six great Chin-han states held a great council and agreed to merge their separate fiefs into a kingdom. They named the capital of the new kingdom Su-ya-bul, whence the present word Seoul is probably derived, and it was situated where Kyong-ju now stands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They placed upon the throne a boy of thirteen years named Hyuk-ku-se with the royal title Ku-se-gan. The story of his advent is typically Korean: a company of revellers beheld upon a mountainside a ball of light on which a horse was seated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they approached, the horse rose straight into the air and disappeared, leaving a great luminous egg. This soon opened of itself and disclosed a handsome boy, the wonder accompanied by vivid light and the noise of thunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Alyong, the Bird-Bill Bride of the Spring

region.zh: 南泉井，慶州（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Silla founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 53 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6 & 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: Beside the Yun-yung Spring a hen raises her wing and from her side comes forth a female child with a mouth like a bird's bill; washed in the spring, the bill falls off and she becomes like other children, so the well is named Pal-ch'un, the Falling of the Bill. In the fifth year of his reign the boy-king Hyokkose espouses her, and Koreans see in them the perfect marriage; when he dies she follows him within seven days, so completely were they one.
summary.zh: 閼英井（雲慶井）畔有雞開翼，自肋下出一女嬰，喙如鳥嘴；浴於井水而喙落，乃如常兒，井因名泊蓮（喙落）。赫居世王五年迎娶之，國人視為夫婦之範。王薨七日，后亦隨逝，若不能獨存者。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic legend; 'resurrection' tagged loosely for the joint-death motif, interpretively.

passages.text: Not long after the wonder of the luminous egg another was seen. Beside the Yun-yung Spring a hen raised her wing, and from her side came forth a female child with a mouth like a bird's bill; but when they washed her in the spring the bill fell off and left her like other children. For this reason the well was named the Pal-ch'un, which refers to the falling of the bill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another tradition says that she was formed from the rib of a dragon which inhabited the spring. In the fifth year of his reign the youthful king espoused this girl, and they typify to all Koreans the perfect marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In 4 AD Hyuk-ku-se, the wise king of Sil-la, died, and seven days later his queen followed him. It is said that they were so completely one that neither could live without the other. Nam-ha his son built a shrine to his father and reigned in his stead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Frog under the Boulder

region.zh: 北夫餘林溪（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Buyeo origin legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 50 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: King Ha-bu-ru of North Pu-yu grieves that Providence has given him no son. Riding in the forest he prays to the Great Spirit at a rushing stream; his horse stands with bowed head before a great boulder, tears rolling down its face. He turns the boulder over and finds beneath it a child of the color of gold in the form of a toad, and names him Keum-wa, Golden Toad. Soon after, the kingdom removes to East Pu-yu, near Paektu Mountain.
summary.zh: 北夫餘王解夫婁無子，乘馬獵於林，至急流之畔祈天求嗣。馬低首立於巨石之前，淚落如雨。王翻其石，得金色蛙形之兒，乃名金蛙。未幾國遷於東夫餘，近白頭山之地。

sensitivity.note: Buyeo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: It must have been about fifty years before the beginning of our era that King Ha-bu-ru sat upon the throne of North Pu-yu. His great sorrow was that Providence had not given him a son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Riding one day in the forest he reached the bank of a swift rushing stream, and there dismounting he besought the Great Spirit to grant him a son. Turning to remount, he found the horse standing with bowed head before a great boulder while tears were rolling down its face. He turned the boulder over and found beneath it a child of the color of gold, with a form resembling a toad. Thus was his prayer answered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took the curious child home and gave it the name Keum-wa, Golden Toad. Soon after this the kingdom removed to East Pu-yu, near the White Head Mountain, known as Pak-tu San.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Jumong Outwits the Royal Stables

region.zh: 東夫餘王廄（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Goguryeo founding cycle from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 40 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The egg-born archer boy Chu-mong is no favorite at court, and his rivals seek his death; the king makes him keeper of the royal stables. Like Jacob of Holy Writ he turns wits to the situation: by fattening the poorer horses and starving the good ones he reserves the fleetest steeds for himself, so that in every hunt he leads the rout and secures the lion's share of the game — and earns the mortal hatred of his seven brothers.
summary.zh: 卵生神箭童子朱蒙不見喜於宮中，仇家欲害之；王乃命其掌王廄。彼如雅各弄智，故意肥劣馬而瘦良馬，暗留駿足自乘，故每獵必先馳而多獲。七兄弟由此恨之入骨，共謀殺之。

sensitivity.note: Goguryeo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The egg at last burst and disclosed a fine boy. This precocious youth at seven years of age was so expert with the bow that he won the name of Chu-mong, the Skillful Archer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was not a favorite with the people, and they tried to compass his death; but the king protected him and made him keeper of the royal stables. Like Jacob of Holy Writ he brought his wits to bear upon the situation: by fattening the poorer horses and making the good ones lean, he succeeded in reserving for his own use the fleetest steeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus in the hunt he always led the rout and secured the lion's share of the game. For this his seven brothers hated him and determined upon his death; by night his mother sought his bedside and whispered the word of warning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Yuri and the Broken Sword-Blade

region.zh: 夫餘市井（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Goguryeo founding cycle from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 19 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Chu-mong fled south he left behind a wife and son, Yuri. Playing with pebbles in the street, Yuri breaks a woman's water jar; her taunt — you are a child without a father — drives the boy to seek a knife for self-destruction before his mother reveals the truth: his father is a great king in the south, who hid a token under a tree. Wearied by searching, Yuri sits in despair until he hears a picking sound from a house post; digging beneath it he unearths half a broken blade, carries it south, and when the halves match, his father proclaims him heir.
summary.zh: 朱蒙南奔，留妻與子類利。類利戲於市以礫石，誤碎汲者水甕；婦人怒斥：『無父之子！』類利慚欲自裁，母乃告以實情：父為南方大王，去時留信物於樹下。類利遍尋不獲，倦極坐於屋後，忽聞柱中有剝啄之聲，曰：『此樹也！』掘柱下得斷劍之半。負劍南下，父子各持其半，合之而吻合，遂立為儲君。

sensitivity.note: Token-recognition episode parallels wide-spread broken-token heirship tales; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: When Chu-mong fled southward from Pu-yu he left behind him a wife and son, the latter named Yu-ri. Tradition says that one day while playing with pebbles in the street he accidentally broke a woman's water jar. In anger she exclaimed, 'You are a child without a father.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy went sadly home and asked his mother if it was true. She answered yes, to see what the boy would do. He went out and found a knife and was on the point of plunging it into his body when she threw herself upon him, saying: 'Your father is living and is a great king in the south. Before he left he hid a token under a tree, which you are to find and take to him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy searched everywhere but could not find the tree. At last, wearied out, he sat down behind the house in despair, when suddenly he heard a sound as of picking, coming from one of the posts of the house, and said, 'This is the tree, and I shall now find the token.' Digging beneath the post he unearthed the broken blade of a sword.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: With this he started south, and when he reached his father's palace he showed the token. His father produced the other half of the broken blade, and as the two matched he received the boy and proclaimed him heir to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Onjo and Biryu Found Baekje

region.zh: 漢江流域，稷山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Baekje founding legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 18 BC

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Yuri appears as heir, Chu-mong's younger sons Biryu and Onjo flee southward. Ascending Sam-gak San behind Seoul they survey the land: Biryu chooses the western coast at Mi-ch'u-hol, Onjo goes directly south to Chik-san, where the king of Ma-han grants him land. Biryu finds his settlement sterile and unhealthy and rejoins his brother, then dies of chagrin at his failure; Onjo sets up the little kingdom of South Pu-yu, which history knows as Paek-je.
summary.zh: 類利立為儲，朱蒙別子沸流、溫祚懼而南奔。登首爾背後之三角山，望野而議：沸流取海濱彌鄒忽之地，溫祚南徑至稷山。馬韓王賜溫祚膏腴之地，遂建小國，號南夫餘。沸流所居地瘠氣惡，乃復歸其弟，旋因愧恨而卒。國名百濟，或謂始名十濟，後以眾增而改。

sensitivity.note: Baekje dynastic founding legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Yu-ri had two half-brothers, Pi-ryu and On-jo, sons of a wife Chu-mong had taken more recently. When Yu-ri appeared on the scene these two brothers, knowing how proverbially unsafe the head of a king's relative is, feared for their lives and fled southward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ascending Sam-gak San, the mountain immediately behind the present Seoul, they surveyed the country southward. Pi-ryu the elder chose the country along the sea, settling at Mi-ch'u-hol, now In-ch'un; On-jo struck southward into what is now Ch'ung-ch'ung Province and settled at Eui-rye-sung, now the district of Chik-san. There he was given a generous tract of land by the king of Ma-han, and set up a little kingdom which he named South Pu-yu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The origin of the name Paek-je is not definitely known. Some say it was because a hundred men constituted the whole of On-jo's party; others say it was at first called Sip-je, and changed to Paek-je when the numbers were swelled by Pi-ryu's party. The latter had found the land sterile and the climate unhealthy at Mi-ch'u-hol, and so was constrained to join his brother again. Not long after he rejoined him he died of chagrin at his own failure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Autumn Gathering in the Susin Cave

region.zh: 神穴，嶺東山間（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ethnographic tradition on Goguryeo rites, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); describing customs of the early centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: The worship of spirits is universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu. Every autumn a great religious festival gathers the tribes in the eastern part of the peninsula at a famous cave called Su-sin, where singing and drinking fill the night — and at the same time the captives are set free.
summary.zh: 高句麗之俗，舉國事神。歲秋大祭，嶺東部族會於神穴，歌飲連宵，並縱囚徒以祓不祥。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of Goguryeo religious customs; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The worship of spirits was universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the autumn there was a great religious festival. In the eastern part of the peninsula there was a famous cave called Su-sin where a great religious gathering occurred each autumn. Their religious rites included singing and drinking, and at the same time captives were set free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bullock Slain for Omens before Battle

region.zh: 高句麗軍營（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ethnographic tradition on Goguryeo rites, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); describing customs of the early centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: On the eve of battle the men of Ko-gu-ryu slaughter a bullock and examine its body for omens, reading the fate of the coming fight in the carcass before they march.
summary.zh: 高句麗人臨戰，必屠牛祭神，驗其臟腑以觀吉凶，然後進兵。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of Goguryeo divination customs; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The worship of spirits was universal among the people of Ko-gu-ryu, and their religious rites included singing, drinking, and the freeing of captives at the autumn festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They worshipped likewise on the eve of battle, slaughtering a bullock and examining the body for omens, reading the fate of the coming contest in the carcass before they marched.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Escaped Pig that Found a Capital

region.zh: 骨乃，楚山附近（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Goguryeo annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 2

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: The king of Ko-gu-ryu is about to sacrifice a pig to his gods when the animal escapes and is chased by the courtier Sul-chi into the district of Kung-na. Catching it near Wi-na Cliff, Sul-chi returns and describes the place as rough, rich in deer, fish and turtles, and therefore suited for a capital. The king moves his court there, and the city remains the capital for two hundred and six years.
summary.zh: 高句麗王將祭神，豕忽逸去，臣燧追至骨乃界、威那崖畔而獲之。歸述其地山川險阻、麋鹿魚鱉甚眾，宜為國都。王遂遷都於彼，凡二百零六年。

sensitivity.note: Goguryeo annal anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: We read that in 2 AD the king of Ko-gu-ryu was about to sacrifice a pig to his gods, when the pig escaped and, taking to its heels, was chased by the courtier Sul-chi into the district of Kung-na. He caught the animal near Wi-na Cliff, north of the Ch'o-san of today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he returned he described the place to the king as being rough and consequently suitable for the site of a capital; deer, fish and turtles also abounded there. He gave such a glowing account that the king moved his capital to that place, where it remained for two hundred and six years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Seok Talhae, the Egg that Drifted across the Japan Sea

region.zh: 阿珍浦，新羅海濱（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Silla annal legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated early first century AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the kingdom of Ta-p'a-ra in northeastern Japan a woman pregnant for seven years brings forth an egg. The neighbors think it an omen and would destroy it, but the mother wraps it in silk and cotton, sets it in a strong chest and commits it to the Japan Sea. The chest drifts to A-jin Harbor on the Silla coast, where an old fisherwoman draws it ashore and finds a beautiful child. Magpies follow the boy in flocks wherever he goes, giving him the name Suk, from the word for magpie, with Tal for 'to put off' from the egg and Ha for the fishwife who opened the chest. The child becomes a giant in body and mind, enters the service of the statesman Pyo-gong, marries the king's daughter and becomes vicegerent of Silla.
summary.zh: 東方旦伐羅國有孕七歲之婦，產一卵。鄰人以為不祥將毀之，母乃以繒裹卵納諸櫝，投於海中。櫝浮至新羅阿珍浦，老嫗取而剖之，得一兒。兒行處，喜鵲隨而翔集，故名鵲（昔）；脫者，出卵也；解者，嫗剖櫝也。兒長成魁偉多智，事大臣瓢公，尚王女，遂為新羅執政。

sensitivity.note: Silla dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Somewhere in north-eastern Japan there was a kingdom known as Ta-p'a-ra, and there a woman, pregnant for seven years, brought forth an egg. The neighbors thought it a bad omen and were minded to destroy it, but the mother, aware of their intentions, wrapped the egg in silk and cotton and, placing it in a strong chest, committed it to the waters of the Japan Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time it drifted to A-jin Harbor on the coast of Sil-la, where an old fisherwoman drew it ashore and found upon opening it a beautiful child. She adopted him and reared him in her humble home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was noticed that wherever the child went the magpies followed him in flocks, so they gave him the name of Suk, the first part of the Chinese word for magpie; Tal means 'to put off', for his having broken forth from the egg, and Ha means 'to open', for the fishwife opened the chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy developed into a giant both physically and mentally. His foster-mother gave him what education she could afford and then sent him to enter the service of the great statesman Pyo-gong, who recognized his merit and introduced him at court. His rise was so rapid that he married the king's daughter and became vicegerent of the realm, the king resigning into his hands the greater part of the business of state.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kyon-mo-ju Weds the Being from the Sky

region.zh: 伽倻山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gaya founding legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated legendary antiquity

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: Of the five Gaya states subject to Ka-rak, the founder of one is known: he was descended from Kyon-mo-ju, the female divinity of Ka-ya Mountain, who wedded the celestial being Yi-ja-ga. Their offspring, Yi-i-a-si, founded one of the Gaya states — a union of mountain goddess and sky being at the root of a polity.
summary.zh: 加羅所屬五伽倻，其一之祖可考：乃伽倻山女神己慕主與天人夷刀伽所生。其子悅己斯遂建一伽倻之國，山神天人之合，遂啟一方之業。

sensitivity.note: Gaya dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Ka-rak had five dependencies, the districts known under the common name of Ka-ya. Of these Ka-ya states we know the founder of only one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was descended from Kyon-mo-ju, the female divinity of Ka-ya Mountain, who wedded a celestial being, Yi-ja-ga. Their offspring, Yi-i-a-si, founded one of the Ka-ya states.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Serpent of Su-ro's Grave

region.zh: 首露王陵，金海（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Gaya legend recorded in Korean annals, cited in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 935 and later

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 7, eBook #52127

summary.en: When Silla falls in 935, worthless wretches defile the grave of Keum Su-ro, founder of Ka-rak — and are mysteriously killed, one by a falling beam, one by an invisible archer, and nine others by a serpent eighteen feet long. Three centuries later Japanese invaders who open the same tomb find vast store of gold and jade, a skull of prodigious size, and beside the body two women whose features are preserved but dissolve when exposed to the air.
summary.zh: 新羅亡時（935年），有匪徒盜掘駕洛國始祖首露王陵，旋遭橫死：一為梁壓，一為無形弓矢所射，餘九人皆為十八尺大蛇所噬。三百年後日軍再掘其墓，得金玉甚富，王顱異常巨大，屍側二女面貌如生，見風而化。

sensitivity.note: Tomb-guardian-serpent legend; 'resurrection' tagged loosely for the incorrupt-dead motif; interpretively.

passages.text: It is also affirmed that when Sil-la fell in 935, some worthless wretches who defiled the grave of Keum Su-ro were mysteriously killed, one by the falling of a beam, one by an invisible archer, and nine others by a serpent eighteen feet long.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The records say that when the Japanese, at the time of the great invasion three centuries ago, dug open this king's grave, they found great store of gold and jade. The skull of the monarch was of prodigious size, and beside his body lay two women whose features were well preserved but which dissolved and melted away when exposed to the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 7 (1905); not verbatim.
